extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemakers, administrative lawyers, public-interest advocates, and scholars interested in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and evaluating public comments submitted in notice-and-comment rulemaking, with special attention to value-laden comments and mass/form-letter campaigns. Emphasizes how agencies should treat technical, value-based, and mass-submitted comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value-laden / policy-preference comments should receive consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Value-laden comments expressing policy preferences should not be systematically discounted; agencies must give weight to value preferences expressed in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mendelson's central principle: values matter to democratic legitimacy. While technical/scientific input is important, agency decisionmaking should also account for expressed values rather than excluding them as 'non-technical' or 'uninformed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/scientific comments should be weighted but not exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical and scientific comments deserve heavy weighting in agency consideration, but they should not be treated as the sole category worthy of consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mendelson concedes the importance of technical/scientific input but argues agencies should avoid an exclusive focus that sidelines value-based public input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass campaigns (form letters) should at least trigger agency investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A torrent of mass comments—even if duplicative—should prompt the agency to investigate whether it has mis-estimated public preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass comments can act as a 'fire alarm' signaling potential errors in agency assessment of public views. Agencies should not automatically dismiss mass submissions as a single comment; they should evaluate whether further inquiry is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit the underlying value or policy preference
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-formed value-laden comment should explicitly state the underlying value or policy preference at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t merely assert a position; identify the value (e.g., public health, environmental protection) the commenter is seeking to advance so the agency can see the normative basis for the comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect the stated value to the agency's statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should connect the articulated value or policy preference to the agency's statutory authority (e.g., identifying how a statute's purpose supports the value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete legal linkages — for example, explain how the Clean Air Act's purpose (public health) bears on the rule and why the proposed rule conflicts with that statutory purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate why the agency is required to weigh that value
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the legal or policy basis obligating the agency to consider the value (statutory text, legislative history, Executive Orders, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant statutory provisions, legislative history, executive guidance, or judicial precedent that demonstrate the agency must give weight to the value being asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate the scope/scale of who shares the value preference
rubrics_metrics.description: State the scope or scale of those who share the value preference (e.g., geographic or numerical scope of affected persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quantification or concrete descriptors (e.g., 'this comment reflects the views of X residents living within Y miles of facilities') to help the agency assess how widespread the concern is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include at least some unique factual or value content per comment in mass campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass-comment design should ensure each submission contains some unique factual or value content so it can be coded as substantive rather than purely duplicative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in form-letter campaigns, add individualized facts or localized details (locations, personal experiences, demographic information) to increase the likelihood each comment will be treated substantively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct commenters to a specific decision the agency must make
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass campaigns should instruct commenters to focus on a particular agency decision point that the rulemaking will resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear direction about the decision at issue makes it easier for agencies to map comments to discrete policy choices and to determine whether further inquiry or analysis is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the agency with a quantifiable basis for further inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments (or campaigns) should give agencies quantifiable information that supports follow-up investigation (sample sizes, geographic distribution, demographics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply data or methodological details that allow the agency to assess representativeness and to design targeted fact-finding (e.g., how many commenters from a region, demographic breakdowns, or sampling methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating individual lay/value comments as inherently uninformed
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual lay comments that express values should not be automatically discounted as uninformed; they should be assessed on their substantive contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate such comments for factual content, legal connections, and articulated reasons rather than dismissing them solely because they come from non-experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design mass-comment campaigns to maximize investigatory value
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns should be structured to trigger agency attention and legitimate follow-up, not merely to register large numbers of identical submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine quantities (lots of submissions) with quality (unique points, data, and links to decision points) so the agency has cause and means to investigate the concerns raised.
